title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description:
# Longest Increasing Subsequence

Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest **strictly increasing subsequence**.

A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more elements without changing the order of the remaining elements. The chosen numbers do not need to be contiguous, but every next chosen number must be larger than the previous chosen number.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** One longest increasing subsequence is [2,3,7,101].

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [0,1,0,3,2,3]
**Output:** 4
**Explanation:** One valid subsequence is [0,1,2,3]. Equal values cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence.

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [7,7,7,7,7,7,7]
**Output:** 1

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 2500`
* `-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4`

solutions.name: Quadratic DP Ending at Each Index
solutions.description:
## Approach
Let `dp[i]` be the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that must end at index `i`. For every earlier index `j`, if `nums[j] < nums[i]`, extend the best chain ending at `j` into `i`.

## Key Insight
The state is tied to the final chosen element, not to a contiguous window. The answer is the maximum over all ending positions because the best subsequence may end anywhere in the array.

## Complexity Analysis
The nested scan checks every ordered pair of indices, so the time complexity is O(n^2). The `dp` table stores one length per index, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Patience Sorting Tails
solutions.description:
## Approach
Maintain `tails[length - 1]` as the smallest possible tail value for any increasing subsequence of that length. For each number, binary search the first tail greater than or equal to it and replace that tail.

## Key Insight
`tails` is not necessarily one real subsequence; it is a set of best tail candidates. Replacing with the first value greater than or equal to the current number preserves strictness and keeps future extension options as small as possible.

## Complexity Analysis
Each of the n numbers performs one binary search over the current tail list, so the time complexity is O(n log n). The tail array can grow to length n, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Top-Down Include-or-Skip Memoization
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use recursion on the current index and the previously chosen index. At each position, either skip the current number or take it when it is larger than the previous chosen value, then memoize the best result for that state.

## Key Insight
The brute-force subsequence search branches at every element, but the only information needed for the future is the current index and the previous chosen index. Memoization collapses repeated suffix decisions into O(n^2) states.

## Complexity Analysis
There are O(n^2) `(index, previous)` states and each state does O(1) work besides recursive calls. The memo table also stores O(n^2) values.

solutions.name: Fenwick Tree with Coordinate Compression
solutions.description:
## Approach
Sort and deduplicate the values to give each number a rank. A Fenwick tree stores the best LIS length for rank prefixes; for the current number, query ranks strictly smaller than its rank and then update its rank with the new length.

## Key Insight
Strictly increasing means equal values must not feed each other, so the query uses `rank - 1`. The Fenwick tree stores maximums rather than sums, turning value-order DP into prefix maximum queries.

## Complexity Analysis
Coordinate compression takes O(n log n), and each query/update takes O(log n). The compressed values and Fenwick tree use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Segment Tree Range-Max DP
solutions.description:
## Approach
Compress values to ranks and keep a segment tree where each rank stores the best LIS length ending with that value. For each number, query the maximum over all smaller ranks, add one, and update the current rank.

## Key Insight
The recurrence is `bestEndingAtValue = 1 + max(bestEndingAtSmallerValue)`. A segment tree makes that range maximum explicit and is easier to extend when the query range later becomes a custom interval.

## Complexity Analysis
Sorting for compression costs O(n log n), and every range query and point update costs O(log n). The segment tree uses O(n) space after compression.

tests.description: Canonical mixed array where the longest increasing subsequence has length four.
Repeated values and later growth verify that subsequences are not required to be contiguous.
All values equal, so a strictly increasing subsequence can contain only one element.
Single-element boundary has LIS length one.
Strictly decreasing input cannot build any increasing chain longer than one.
Strictly increasing input uses every element.
Longer mixed sequence tests the patience-sorting tail replacement invariant.
A later smaller value must replace a tail so that [3,8,9] can be found.
Negative values still follow the same strict ordering rule.
Coordinate compression routes must handle negative values and later low restarts.
Equal values cannot chain, but a later larger value can extend one of them.
A dense zigzag case checks that tails and range maximum structures keep the best future option.
A local dip should replace a tail without losing the length-four answer.
